classification.difficultyReason: Establish triangle congruence and use corresponding sides to prove a second triangle is isosceles.

content.prompt: In the diagram to the right, $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles with $AB=AC$, $BD\perp AC$ and $CE\perp AB$.

spec.description: Isosceles triangle ABC with A above horizontal BC. E and D are perpendicular feet on AB and AC respectively; BD and CE cross. Right-angle marks occupy BDC and BEC. ED is deliberately absent, as in the source. Ordinary source blue strokes are rendered black under house style.
spec.mathematics: AB=AC; D lies on AC with BD perpendicular to AC; E lies on AB with CE perpendicular to AB.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens, vertex labels and perpendicular markers are visible.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that $\triangle BDC$ is congruent to $\triangle CEB$.

answer.short: $\triangle BDC\equiv\triangle CEB$ (AAS): equal right angles, equal base angles and common side $BC$.
answer.worked:
In $\triangle BDC$ and $\triangle CEB$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BDC&=\angle CEB=90^\circ &&\text{(perpendicular lines)}\\\angle DCB&=\angle EBC &&\text{(base angles of isosceles }\triangle ABC\text{)}\\BC&=CB &&\text{(common side)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle BDC\equiv\triangle CEB$ (AAS).

answer.short:
$AE=AD$, so $\triangle AED$ is isosceles.

Subtract the equal corresponding sides $BE=CD$ from $AB=AC$.
answer.worked:
From part a, $BE=CD$ (matching sides of congruent triangles). Since $E$ lies on $AB$ and $D$ lies on $AC$:
$$\begin{align*}AE&=AB-BE\\AD&=AC-CD.\end{align*}$$
But $AB=AC$ (given) and $BE=CD$, so $AE=AD$. Therefore $\triangle AED$ is isosceles.
